## Solution

Let $\{e^{n+1}_{\alpha}\}_{\alpha\in J}$ be the $(n+1)$-cells of the relative CW-complex $(X,A)$, with characteristic maps
$$\Phi_\alpha : (D^{n+1},\, S^n) \longrightarrow (X_{n+1},\, X_n)$$
and attaching maps $\varphi_\alpha := \Phi_\alpha\big|_{S^n} : S^n \to X_n$.

### Definition of the obstruction cochain

Define
$$\boxed{\theta^{n+1}(g) \in C^{n+1}(X,A;\,\pi_n Y), \qquad \theta^{n+1}(g)\big(e^{n+1}_\alpha\big) \;=\; \big[\,g\circ\varphi_\alpha\,\big] \;\in\; \pi_n(Y).}$$

That is, the cochain evaluates on each $(n+1)$-cell by composing the attaching map of that cell with $g$, and taking the homotopy class of the resulting map $S^n \to Y$.

### Well-definedness (uses $n$-simplicity)

A priori, $g\circ\varphi_\alpha : S^n \to Y$ represents an element of $\pi_n(Y, y_0)$ where $y_0 = g(\varphi_\alpha(s_0))$ for a chosen basepoint $s_0\in S^n$. Changing the basepoint $s_0$ to $s_1$ identifies $\pi_n(Y,y_0)$ with $\pi_n(Y,y_1)$ via the path $g\circ\varphi_\alpha(\text{path }s_0\to s_1)$ in $Y$, and the resulting identification depends on the homotopy class of that path—i.e., on the $\pi_1(Y)$-action on $\pi_n(Y)$.

Since $Y$ is **$n$-simple**, $\pi_1(Y)$ acts trivially on $\pi_n(Y)$, so the local coefficient system $\{\pi_n(Y,y)\}_{y\in Y}$ is simple (constant). Hence $[g\circ\varphi_\alpha]$ is a well-defined element of the single group $\pi_n(Y)$, independent of all basepoint choices. This gives a well-defined cochain $\theta^{n+1}(g)\in C^{n+1}(X,A;\pi_n Y)$.

### Vanishing if and only if $g$ extends to $X_{n+1}$

($\Longrightarrow$) Suppose $\theta^{n+1}(g)=0$, i.e., $[g\circ\varphi_\alpha]=0\in\pi_n(Y)$ for every $\alpha$. Then each $g\circ\varphi_\alpha : S^n\to Y$ is null-homotopic, so there exists a homotopy $H_\alpha : S^n\times I\to Y$ with $H_\alpha(-,0)=g\circ\varphi_\alpha$ and $H_\alpha(-,1)=\text{const}$. By the homotopy extension property applied to the pair $(D^{n+1},S^n)$, a null-homotopy of $g\circ\varphi_\alpha$ is equivalent to an extension $\tilde g_\alpha : D^{n+1}\to Y$ with $\tilde g_\alpha\big|_{S^n}=g\circ\varphi_\alpha$. Defining $\tilde g$ on $X_{n+1}$ by $\tilde g\big|_{X_n}=g$ and $\tilde g\big|_{e^{n+1}_\alpha}=\tilde g_\alpha\circ\Phi_\alpha^{-1}$ gives a continuous extension $X_{n+1}\to Y$.

($\Longleftarrow$) Suppose $g$ extends to $\tilde g : X_{n+1}\to Y$. Then for each $\alpha$, the restriction $\tilde g\circ\Phi_\alpha : D^{n+1}\to Y$ is an extension of $g\circ\varphi_\alpha$ over the disk. A map $S^n\to Y$ extends over $D^{n+1}$ if and only if it is null-homotopic, so $[g\circ\varphi_\alpha]=0\in\pi_n(Y)$ for every $\alpha$, hence $\theta^{n+1}(g)=0$. $\blacksquare$

### Summary

The obstruction cochain is the cellular $(n+1)$-cochain
$$\theta^{n+1}(g)\big(e^{n+1}_\alpha\big) = [\,g\circ\varphi_\alpha\,]\in\pi_n(Y),$$
assigning to each $(n+1)$-cell the homotopy class of $g$ precomposed with that cell's attaching map. The $n$-simplicity of $Y$ makes this well-defined with constant coefficients. It vanishes as a cochain precisely when every $g\circ\varphi_\alpha$ is null-homotopic, which is precisely the condition that $g$ extends over each $(n+1)$-cell, i.e., that $g$ extends to a map $X_{n+1}\to Y$.
